en: To regard something as caused by; a quality or feature
hook: ATTRIBUTE: give TRIBUTE (credit) to the cause.
story: Attribute. One summer, Mahin's mango tree suddenly produced twice as much fruit as usual. His father attributed it to the new fertiliser; his mother attributed it to her daily prayers; the neighbour attributed it to pure luck. To attribute is to regard something as caused by a particular source. As a noun, stressed on the first syllable, an attribute is a quality or feature: patience is a fine attribute in a teacher. Synonyms: ascribe, credit, assign.

gre.s: Although the coach was quick to ____ the team's victory to his new training regimen, most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders.
gre.clue: most observers credited the opposing goalkeeper's uncharacteristic blunders

en: Causing great disaster or misfortune
hook: CALAMITOUS: a CALAMITY.
story: Calamitous. In November 1970, the Bhola cyclone struck the coast of what is now Bangladesh. In a single night, a wall of seawater swept away entire villages, and hundreds of thousands of people died. Historians call it one of the most calamitous storms ever recorded: causing great disaster and terrible misfortune. A calamity is a disaster; calamitous describes anything that brings one. A calamitous decision can ruin lives or fortunes. Synonyms: disastrous, catastrophic, devastating.

gre.s: What began as a minor accounting error proved ____ for the firm: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate.
gre.clue: within a year it had lost its largest clients, its reputation, and finally its license to operate

en: To examine and remove objectionable parts from media
hook: CENSOR: CUTS out what's forbidden. Not censure (criticize).
story: Censor. Under a military government, a newspaper editor had to send his pages to a government office every night. Officers read each article and cut any line that criticised the rulers. Some mornings, the paper appeared with blank white columns. The officers were censoring the news: examining it and removing parts they considered objectionable. A censor is also the person who does this. Do not confuse censor with censure, which means to criticise harshly. Synonyms: suppress, redact, expurgate.

gre.s: Rather than ____ the novel's explicit passages, as the publisher had demanded, the author withdrew the manuscript entirely, insisting that every word remain intact.
gre.clue: insisting that every word remain intact

en: To publicly support or fight for a cause
hook: GRE trick: to CHAMPION a cause means to fight FOR it.
story: Champion. When the local council planned to fill in an old pond in Mymensingh to build a market, a retired schoolteacher named Rumana refused to stay quiet. She wrote letters to newspapers, organised students, and spoke at every public meeting. Thanks to her, the pond survived. She had championed its cause: publicly supported and fought for it. As a verb, to champion means to defend a cause, not to win a trophy. Synonyms: advocate, espouse, defend.

gre.s: Though she was initially skeptical of renewable energy, the senator went on to ____ it more vigorously than any of her colleagues, sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power.
gre.clue: sponsoring dozens of bills to expand solar power

en: To make a problem worse
hook: GRE trick: COMPOUND interest grows; a COMPOUNDED problem grows worse.
story: Compound. Zayan dented his father's car in a minor bump. Instead of confessing, he hid the damage and later blamed a rickshaw. When the truth came out a week later, his father was far angrier about the lie than about the dent. Zayan had compounded his mistake: made a bad situation worse. In GRE English, to compound a problem means to add to it, just as compound interest piles interest on top of interest. Synonyms: aggravate, exacerbate, worsen.

gre.s: The governor's initial delay in ordering an evacuation was a serious error, but her subsequent refusal to admit it served only to ____ the damage to her reputation.
gre.clue: her subsequent refusal to admit it

en: To discourage someone from doing something, usually by fear
hook: DETER: like a TERROR that keeps you away.
story: Deter. A string of burglaries hit the flats on Tanvir's street in Uttara. The building owners installed bright lights, cameras, and a large sign: "This building is watched day and night." The burglaries stopped. The cameras had deterred the thieves: discouraged them, usually through fear of the consequences. A deterrent is something that deters, like a heavy fine for littering. The Latin root means to frighten away, the same root as terror. Synonyms: discourage, dissuade, daunt.

gre.s: Lawmakers hoped that steeper fines would ____ drivers from using their phones at the wheel, but accident rates remained unchanged a year later.
gre.clue: hoped that steeper fines would

en: Skillful, especially with the hands
hook: DEXTEROUS: DEXTER is Latin for right hand, the skilled hand.
story: Dexterous. At a roadside stall in Old Dhaka, an old man repairs mobile phones with tools no bigger than toothpicks. His fingers move so quickly that customers lean in to watch: a tiny screw here, a wire soldered there, and the screen glows again. He is dexterous: skillful, especially with the hands. Dexter is Latin for right hand, so dexterity was once right-handed skill. The word can describe a quick mind as well. Synonyms: deft, nimble, adroit.

gre.s: Though his eyesight was failing, the elderly watchmaker remained remarkably ____, able to reassemble a tiny movement of a hundred parts without a single wasted motion.
gre.clue: without a single wasted motion

en: A formal or authoritative statement; a short saying
hook: DICTUM: what is DICTATED, spoken (dictus).
story: Dictum. Every new reporter at a Dhaka newspaper hears the same dictum from the chief editor on the first day: "If your mother says she loves you, check it out." He repeats it at every meeting until it becomes a reflex. A dictum is a formal or authoritative statement, often a short saying that guides practice. It comes from the Latin dicere, to say, as in dictate and dictionary. Courts also issue dicta, their formal remarks. Synonyms: maxim, pronouncement, edict.

gre.s: The founder's ____ that the customer is always right was treated by her managers as an unquestionable law, though she herself frequently ignored it.
gre.clue: treated by her managers as an unquestionable law

en: Conscientiously fulfilling one's duties
hook: DUTIFUL: full of DUTY.
story: Dutiful. Every morning before work, Rahim walks to his parents' house, buys their medicine, checks their blood pressure, and pays their bills. He has done this for twelve years without a single complaint. Neighbours call him a dutiful son: one who conscientiously fulfils his duties and obligations. Dutiful can also hint at doing something because one must rather than from passion, as in the dutiful applause after a dull speech. Synonyms: conscientious, devoted, obedient.

gre.s: A ____ civil servant, she never missed a deadline in thirty years, though colleagues noted that she seemed to take little pleasure in her work.
gre.clue: never missed a deadline in thirty years

en: Able to understand and share the feelings of others
hook: EMPATHETIC: feeling IN (em) someone else's pain (pathos).
story: Empathetic. When Sara failed her driving test, most friends said, "Never mind, try again." But Ishita sat beside her and said, "I remember how humiliated I felt when I failed mine. It is awful." For the first time that day, Sara felt understood. Ishita was empathetic: able to understand and share the feelings of others. Sympathy is feeling sorry for someone; empathy is feeling with them, as if in their place. Synonyms: understanding, compassionate, sensitive.

gre.s: The best nurses are not only technically skilled but also ____, able to sense a frightened patient's anxiety and respond to it before a word is spoken.
gre.clue: able to sense a frightened patient's anxiety

en: To happen afterward as a result
hook: ENSUE: follows like a SEQUEL.
story: Ensue. At a village wedding, the generator suddenly died in the middle of the feast. Total darkness. Chaos ensued: children shrieked, someone knocked over a pot of borhani, and three uncles shouted instructions at once. To ensue is to happen afterward, as a result. It comes from the Latin for to follow, the same root as sequel and sequence. In the ensuing confusion, someone found a torch, and the meal went on. Synonyms: follow, result, arise.

gre.s: When the dam's floodgates were opened without any warning, panic was bound to ____, and thousands of downstream residents fled their homes in the middle of the night.
gre.clue: thousands of downstream residents fled their homes

en: To understand after much thought
hook: FATHOM: measuring deep water — and deep ideas.
story: Fathom. Nadia's grandmother could not fathom why anyone would pay five hundred taka for a cup of coffee in Gulshan. She turned the receipt over twice, as if the explanation might be printed on the back. To fathom is to understand something after much thought, and it is often used with not: I cannot fathom it. A fathom is also a sailor's measure of depth, about six feet, so to fathom a mystery is to sound its depths. Synonyms: comprehend, grasp.

gre.s: Even after decades of study, physicists struggle to ____ the strange behavior of particles at the quantum level, which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect.
gre.clue: which seems to defy every intuition about cause and effect

en: Open, honest, and direct
hook: FRANK: Frank always tells it straight.
story: Frank. When Shuvo asked his mentor to read his first short story, he hoped for praise. Instead she said, "The opening is dull, the dialogue is stiff, and the ending is borrowed. But the third page is brilliant; build from there." It stung, but it helped. She was frank: open, honest, and direct. Frank once meant free, from the Franks, a free people; frank speech is free of disguise. Synonyms: candid, blunt, forthright.

gre.s: Rather than offering the vague reassurances his patients expected, the doctor was always ____, telling them plainly what their prognosis was even when the news was grim.
gre.clue: telling them plainly what their prognosis was

en: Relevant to the subject
hook: GERMANE: GERMAN relatives belong to the family — relevant.
story: Germane. In a seminar on climate policy, a student raised his hand to talk about the price of cricket tickets. The professor smiled politely. "Interesting, but not germane. Let us stay with sea levels." Germane means relevant to the subject at hand. Lawyers object when testimony is not germane to the case. Think of the germ of the matter: something germane sits close to the core. Opposite: irrelevant, extraneous. Synonyms: relevant, pertinent, apposite.

gre.s: The judge excluded the witness's account of the defendant's childhood, ruling that it was not ____ to the question of whether he had signed the contract.
gre.clue: The judge excluded the witness's account

en: To complain in a bad-tempered, muttering way
hook: GRUMBLE: like a grumbling, rumbling stomach.
story: Grumble. Every morning in the queue for the hostel's single working shower, Rafi grumbles: about the cold water, the broken lock, the student who always takes twenty minutes. He never complains to the provost's office; he just mutters under his breath. To grumble is to complain in a bad-tempered, muttering way. The word even sounds like a rumbling empty stomach. Grumbling is complaint without action. Synonyms: grouse, gripe, mutter.

gre.s: Although the workers continued to ____ about the new schedule among themselves, none of them was willing to raise a formal complaint with management.
gre.clue: none of them was willing to raise a formal complaint with management

en: Unwilling to accept new ideas; narrow and conventional
hook: HIDEBOUND: bound tight in an old HIDE (skin).
story: Hidebound. When a young teacher at Joya's school suggested group projects instead of rote memorisation, the old headmaster refused. "We have taught this way for fifty years. Why change now?" He rejected computers and new textbooks too. He was hidebound: narrow-minded and unwilling to accept new ideas. Originally, hidebound described underfed cattle whose skin clung tightly to their bones, too stiff to grow. Opposite: progressive. Synonyms: conservative, rigid, inflexible.

gre.s: The institute's ____ administrators rejected every proposal for curricular reform, insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough for today's students.
gre.clue: insisting that methods good enough for their grandparents were good enough

en: A person who claims beliefs or virtues they don't follow
hook: HYPOCRITE: a Greek actor (hypokrites), playing a role.
story: Hypocrite. Every Friday, a local leader gave fiery speeches against corruption, demanding honesty from every official. Then a newspaper revealed that he had quietly taken bribes for years to approve building permits. People were furious, not only about the bribes but about the speeches. He was a hypocrite: someone who claims beliefs or virtues that he does not actually follow. In ancient Greek, a hypokrites was a stage actor, someone playing a part. Synonyms: pretender, phony, dissembler.

gre.s: The minister who lectured citizens about saving electricity was exposed as a ____ when reporters discovered that his own residence ran air conditioners day and night.
gre.clue: his own residence ran air conditioners day and night

en: Unwise; likely to cause trouble or offense
hook: IM-POLITIC: NOT POLITIC, not diplomatic.
story: Impolitic. At a job interview, Kamal was asked why he had left his previous company. He answered honestly: "My boss was a fool, and the owners were thieves." It might have been true, but it was impolitic: unwise, and likely to cause trouble or offence. Impolitic means not politic, not prudent. It differs from impolite, which is merely rude; an impolitic remark is a strategic blunder. Synonyms: imprudent, injudicious, ill-advised.

gre.s: Though privately he agreed with the protesters, the ambassador judged it ____ to say so publicly, since doing so would surely offend the host government.
gre.clue: since doing so would surely offend the host government

en: Proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects
hook: INSIDIOUS: sneaks INSIDE you quietly.
story: Insidious. High blood pressure is often called the silent killer. Arif's father felt perfectly healthy for years while the pressure was quietly damaging his heart and kidneys. By the time any symptoms appeared, the harm was serious. The disease was insidious: proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects. The Latin root means to lie in wait, as in an ambush. Rumours, too, can spread insidiously. Synonyms: stealthy, subtle, treacherous.

gre.s: The danger of the pollutant lies in its ____ nature: it accumulates in the body slowly and without symptoms, causing irreversible harm long before it can be detected.
gre.clue: slowly and without symptoms

en: A person who acts as a link between two parties
hook: INTER-MEDIARY: in the MIDDLE between.
story: Intermediary. When two cousins stopped speaking after a fight over their grandfather's land, the family asked their uncle Mahbub to help. For months he carried messages between them, softened their words, and suggested compromises, until finally they agreed. He acted as an intermediary: a person who acts as a link between two parties. Inter means between, and medius means middle: someone in the middle. Brokers are intermediaries in business. Synonyms: mediator, go-between, broker.

gre.s: Because the two governments had no formal diplomatic relations, they were forced to negotiate through a neutral ____, who relayed each side's proposals to the other.
gre.clue: who relayed each side's proposals to the other

en: Accepting what happens without active response or resistance
hook: PASSIVE: lets everything PASS by without acting.
story: Passive. In group discussions, Tania sits quietly while louder classmates take over. When someone presents her idea as his own, she says nothing. When her group skips its share of the work, she does it all herself, without protest. Tania is passive: accepting what happens without active response or resistance. The word comes from the Latin pati, to suffer or endure, as in patient. Its opposite is active or assertive. Synonyms: submissive, acquiescent, inert.

gre.s: Far from being ____ spectators of the reforms, the village women organized committees, petitioned officials, and ultimately shaped how the new laws were enforced.
gre.clue: the village women organized committees, petitioned officials

en: Good-humored teasing
hook: RAILLERY: friends RALLY around you with jokes.
story: Raillery. Whenever Farhan's friends gather at the tea stall after class, the teasing begins. They mock his giant headphones, his love of old Hindi film songs, and the way he always orders three samosas. Farhan laughs loudest of all and gives it right back. This is raillery: good-humoured teasing among friends. It shares a French root with rail, as in to rail against, but raillery is light and friendly, not bitter. Contrast ridicule, which wounds. Synonyms: banter, ribbing.

gre.s: The two old rivals enjoyed a long tradition of affectionate ____, trading gentle jokes about each other's age and failing memory whenever they met.
gre.clue: trading gentle jokes

en: To talk or write at length in a confused, aimless way; to walk aimlessly
hook: RAMBLE: like a RAMBLING road with no destination.
story: Ramble. Asked a simple question about his thesis during his viva, Sabbir began with the history of rice farming, drifted to his grandfather's village, mentioned a cricket match, and returned twenty minutes later without ever answering. His examiners exchanged looks. He was rambling: talking at length in a confused, aimless way. To ramble also means to walk aimlessly, as on a lazy ramble through the countryside. Synonyms: digress, meander, wander.

gre.s: Asked a direct question about the budget, the candidate began to ____, drifting from anecdote to anecdote for ten minutes without ever offering a concrete figure.
gre.clue: drifting from anecdote to anecdote

en: To feel bitterness about unfair treatment
hook: RE-SENT: the insult is SENT back again and again in your mind.
story: Resent. For years, Imran's younger brother got the new clothes, the bigger room, and all the praise, while Imran did the chores. He never said a word, but he resented it deeply: he felt bitter about the unfair treatment. To resent is to feel bitterness or indignation at being treated unfairly. Resentment can simmer quietly for decades. Re means again, and sent comes from the Latin for feel: feeling a hurt again and again. Synonyms: begrudge, grudge.

gre.s: Veteran staff members tended to ____ the newcomers' rapid promotions, which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit.
gre.clue: which they attributed to favoritism rather than to merit

en: Remaining after most has gone
hook: RESIDUAL: the RESIDUE left behind.
story: Residual. After the floodwaters finally drained from Mitu's village, a thin layer of mud remained on every floor, and a faint smell lingered for weeks. That leftover mud was residual: remaining after most of something has gone. A residue is what remains. Even after an apology, there can be residual anger, a little bitterness that has not quite left. Residual income keeps arriving after the work is done. Synonyms: remaining, lingering, leftover.

gre.s: Although the fever subsided within a week, the patient suffered from ____ fatigue that persisted for months after the infection itself had cleared.
gre.clue: after the infection itself had cleared

en: Firm determination; to decide firmly or settle
hook: RESOLVE: a RESOLUTION you stick to.
story: Resolve. After Tanvir failed the bar council exam twice, his friends told him to give up. Instead, he moved into a tiny room near the library, studied ten hours a day, and turned down every wedding invitation for a year. His resolve never weakened: his firm determination. He passed with distinction. As a verb, to resolve means to decide firmly, or to settle a problem, as in resolving a dispute. Synonyms: determination, tenacity, grit.

gre.s: Repeated setbacks only strengthened the climbers' ____: after each failed attempt on the summit, they returned the following season eager to try again.
gre.clue: eager to try again

en: A substitute, especially a person acting in another's place
hook: SURROGATE: a SUBSTITUTE who stands in.
story: Surrogate. When Lamia's parents moved abroad for work, her aunt in Rajshahi raised her. She packed her lunch, attended parent meetings, and sat up with her through every fever. For ten years, her aunt was a surrogate mother: a substitute, someone acting in another's place. In medicine, a surrogate mother carries a baby for others. The word comes from the Latin for to elect in place of another. Synonyms: substitute, proxy, stand-in.

gre.s: Unable to attend the ceremony himself, the ailing laureate sent his daughter as a ____ to accept the award and read the speech he had written.
gre.clue: Unable to attend the ceremony himself

en: To speak or write about in an abusively disparaging manner
hook: VILIFY: make someone a VILLAIN.
story: Vilify. After a young journalist exposed a tax scandal, a group of powerful businessmen launched a campaign against her. Posters called her a traitor; anonymous accounts spread lies about her family. They vilified her: spoke and wrote about her in a viciously insulting way, trying to turn the public against her. Vilify contains vile: to make someone seem vile. It is far stronger than criticise. Opposite: praise, extol. Synonyms: malign, defame, revile.

gre.s: Rival newspapers chose to ____ the reformer, branding her a traitor and inventing scandals, even though her proposals were modest and widely popular.
gre.clue: branding her a traitor and inventing scandals

en: Lacking; not good enough
hook: GRE trick: FOUND WANTING means found lacking, not desiring.
story: Wanting. Rafi's first research paper had good data, but his professor returned it with a single comment: "The analysis is wanting." Rafi was puzzled at first. Then he understood: wanting here means lacking, not good enough. When something is weighed and found wanting, it falls short of a standard. In older English, want meant lack, as in the proverb: for want of a nail, the shoe was lost. Synonyms: deficient, lacking, inadequate.

gre.s: The proposal was praised for its ambition, but on close examination its financial projections were found ____, resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept.
gre.clue: resting on assumptions that no serious economist would accept

en: Intentional; stubbornly determined to do as one wants
hook: WILL-FUL: full of your own WILL.
story: Willful. Rumana's three-year-old nephew refused to wear shoes to the wedding. Shoes were offered, then sandals, then a bribe of chocolate. He sat on the floor and screamed, determined to go barefoot no matter what. He was willful: stubbornly determined to do as he wants. Willful also means intentional, as in willful damage, done on purpose rather than by accident. In British English it is spelled wilful. Synonyms: headstrong, obstinate, deliberate.

gre.s: The court ruled that the company's failure to report the leak was not an innocent oversight but a ____ deception, carried out with full knowledge of the risks.
gre.clue: not an innocent oversight
